title: The Whirlwind
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart admits he has tried for two weeks to log every task in a teaching day and never lasts more than an hour, because hundreds of micro-tasks leave no room for recording, let alone for deeper thinking. He argues this is the central tension of the job: the urgent daily work crowds out the important strategic work, so mastery rarely arrives by accident. He borrows the term 'the whirlwind' from The 4 Disciplines of Execution, whose authors say the day job is the real enemy of executing anything new, and quotes their claim that when urgency and importance clash, urgency wins. His practical turn is aimed at administrators, who he says most underestimate the whirlwind, and he proposes planning strategy with the whirlwind in view and running PD on managing it. A footnote names his own non-whirlwind priority, student motivation, as the thing he believes sits behind burnout.
points: The post supplies a name, 'the whirlwind', for the daily rush of urgent micro-tasks that keeps teachers from pursuing their long-term goals.
Stuart's failed attempt to log every task in a teaching day serves as evidence that the work is too dense to even observe, let alone optimise.
He applies the 4 Disciplines of Execution claim that urgency always beats importance to schools, explaining why good resolutions and new initiatives stall.
He singles out leaders as the people most likely to underestimate the whirlwind and urges them to design strategies and PD with it clearly in view.
The footnote ties the abstract time-management point to a concrete wildly important goal, student ownership and motivation, which he sees as a root cause of attrition.
quotes: There are hundreds of micro-tasks that make up my teaching hours and dozens more that just have to be done during the snippets of time between classes, before school starts, and during my lunch hour.

The trouble, of course, is that in that rush of micro-work, I'm unlikely to create the time and space it takes to reach intellectual breakthroughs [1], or follow-through on goals I set for myself at the start of the year, or continue pushing my limits in one of the six areas of high-leverage work

It's darned if you do, darned if you don't — I need to do the myriad of micro-tasks that make up my day job, but I've got to carve out time for the important, long-term, strategic work, too. That's really what the “secret skills of master teachers” series was about — how do we make decisions today that yield mastery eventually?

The real enemy of execution is your day job! We call it the whirlwind. It's the massive amount of energy that's necessary just to keep your operation going on a day-to-day basis; and, ironically, it's also the thing that makes it so hard to execute anything new. The whirlwind robs from you the focus required to move… forward.

Administrators, take note — the whirlwind is real! Leaders, according to the 4 Disciplines, are the folks most likely to underestimate the time and energy that the whirlwind demands. The solution, of course, is to make all strategies with the whirlwind clearly in view and create professional development sessions solely on how to manage the whirlwind in a better and saner fashion.

I'm more and more convinced that much of what burns us out and keeps us going has to do with student ownership, which is built on student motivation. If we all taught kids who owned their education, then I don't think as many of us would leave — either literally by quitting or essentially by disengaging with our hearts and minds from the work.
